title: Building Reliable AI Agents for Data Teams

segments.text: Welcome everyone.
Today we are talking about building reliable AI agents for data engineering teams.
I'll cover three things: why agents fail in production, how to evaluate them, and how to govern what they can do.
First, why do agents fail? The most common failure is not the model.
It is missing evidence.
An agent that cannot read the pipeline logs will guess, and a confident guess is worse than no answer.
So the first rule is: give agents read-only access to the evidence they need, and nothing more.
The second failure mode is unbounded loops.
Without step and time budgets an agent can call tools forever.
Every execution should have a maximum number of steps, model calls, tool calls, and a timeout.
Third, prompt injection.
Logs, emails and documents can contain instructions written by someone else.
You cannot fix that with a better prompt.
You fix it by keeping authorization outside the model.
The model may ask to restart a pipeline, but a policy engine decides, and a human approves high-risk actions.
Now let's talk about evaluation.
Treat agents like software: write test cases before you ship.
A good suite has functional cases, regression cases, prompt injection cases and failure cases.
For example: what happens when the model provider is down? The agent should fail cleanly, not hang.
Measure task completion, schema compliance, correct tool selection, latency and cost for every version.
And never publish a new version unless it passes the same suite as the old one.
Compare them side by side.
LLM as a judge can be one signal, but it should never be the only gate for quality or safety.
Let me show a quick case study.
A team ran a pipeline diagnostic agent for three months.
In the first week it recommended restarting a pipeline that was failing because of a schema change.
A restart would not have helped.
The approval step caught it, and the team added a regression test.
After that, the agent's recommendations improved because the evaluation suite encoded what good looks like.
Governance is the last piece.
Every agent version should be immutable once published.
Record exactly which model, tools, workflow and policy each execution used, so you can reproduce it.
Keep an audit log that is tamper-evident, and separate who requests an action from who approves it.
Action items for your team: first, inventory the tools your agents can call and classify their risk.
Second, add execution budgets to every agent today.
It takes minutes and prevents runaway costs.
Third, write at least five evaluation cases per agent, including one prompt injection case.
Fourth, require human approval for anything that writes to production systems.
A key term to remember is idempotency: a retried action must not happen twice.
Another is groundedness: every claim in the answer should be supported by retrieved evidence.
To wrap up: give agents evidence, bound their execution, test them like software, and govern their actions.
As one engineer told me, the best agent is the one you can explain at three in the morning.
Thank you.
I'm happy to take questions about evaluation suites and approval workflows.
